subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT ON MOTION FOR PROMOTION OF INTERNATIONAL PEACE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford) moved:
That the recommendations contained in the second report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations, presented to the house on May 19, 1930, be concurred in.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT ON MOTION FOR PROMOTION OF INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext: Could we have an explanation so that we may know what we are dealing with?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT ON MOTION FOR PROMOTION OF INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext:
The report is concerned with the motion, the proposed resolution, of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) as to the desirability of spending one dollar in the promotion of international peace for every one hundred dollars spent in the promotion of war. The committee subjected that resolution to a full analysis, took evidence from Doctor Skelton, Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs; Professor Mackenzie, of Toronto university; Dean Corbett, of McGill university; Mr. Graham Spry, secretary of the Associated Canadian Clubs; and a submission by Doctor Tory, and came to the conclusions set out in the report, first, that the evidence not being as full and complete as might be wished the resolution should be considered at another session of parliament. Secondly, with regard to the contents of the resolution, the feeling of the committee was that the Department of External Affairs, manned at the present time by the Prime Minister of Canada and Doctor Skelton, was doing splendid work in the promotion of peace at home and abroad, and that the machinery and facilities of that department in the way of international peace should be extended and increased. By so doing it was further felt that parliament might see its way clear to increase its grant to the League of Nations Society in Canada. The grant now I believe is S3,000 per annum. The committee felt that that grant should be increased if the League of Nations Society was to do its best work throughout the Dominion in the promotion of international peace in the schools of this country, primary and secondary, and also in the universities of the Dominion.

Another idea mooted before the committee was that it might- be well for parliament to consider the advisability of the establishment of an international library linked up with the Department of External Affaire. If that were done the committee thought that in due time it might be possible to organize a summer school on international relations for Canada with Ottawa as the headquarters.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, those are the main points dealt with in the report, and I now leave it for the house to endorse..

May I bring to the notice of the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) the fact that postal terminal "A", which is the largest postal station in Toronto closes its doors at 7 o'clock every day, except Saturday, when the closing time is at noon. Surely this is not right. I wish to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General also the question of keeping all post offices, especially the larger ones, open till midnight during the Shriners' convention. Postal terminal "A" should be kept open till 10 o'clock. It is beside the mail trains and people coming down with mail find the place closed and cannot get stamps.
The post office is a public utility and the public interest should be paramount. Toronto returns a great profit. Why not give an up-to-date service? The postal revenues of Toronto are about 86,000,000, which shows the need of a large central post office near the depot with proper accommodation for the public using this most important utility.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was kind enough to send me the notice of this question, and during the noon hour I made certain inquiries at the department. Before I read the statement which they prepared for me, may I say that when any large conventions are being organized it would be only right that the department should facilitate as much as possible the work of those conventions in the matter of communication by mail, and on such occasions special arrangements will be made to meet their convenience. Let me read the memorandum prepared by the department:
The department has for some time been giving consideration to the arrangements for postal facilities during the Shriners' convention in June. Special offices are being opened in the government building at the exhibition grounds and in proximity to the two points where accommodation is being provided by the railway companies.
Adequate facilities for conducting postal business will also be in operation in the Royal York hotel, where the headquarters of the convention will be located. This office, which is immediately across Front street from terminal "A," will be open at all hours of the day.
The situation is being closely watched and is being given special study by a competent postal official of the Toronto office. In the event of there being any indication that the arrangements already made will prove inadequate, the department is prepared to take whatever additional steps are necessary to ensure a first-class service.

As regards the hour of closing of postal terminal "A," it may he stated that experience has shown that there is no demand for service at that point after 7 o'clock in the evening. The Adelaide street office, which is more conveniently situated, is open until 10 o'clock every night.
It should be pointed out, however, that while the lobby of terminal ''A" is closed at 7 o'clock, the public can obtain access for the purpose of posting mail matter and purchasing stamps by entering the office on the lower level immediately under the main entrance to the lobby.
As regards the hours of closing of the other postal stations in Toronto, these have been fixed as the result of experience obtained by the officials at Toronto and it is not considered that there is sufficient public demand for later closing to justify the department in going to the extra expense which would be involved if employees had to be retained on duty to serve the wickets.
I may add that the whole situation is now being reviewed again, and if thought necessary the hours will be changed.
FILIPINO IMMIGRATION On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) if he has had any advices as to the influx of Filipinos into British Columbia. According to my information, these Filipinos first invaded the states of California and Oregon. They gave a good deal of trouble in the Sacramento valley. Then quite a number of them moved up to the state of Washington, and as a result there have been some race riots. I believe two hundred or so were driven off the farms between Seattle and Tacoma. Now they are drifting into the province of British Columbia and are entering the labour market. If we do not wish to have another race problem in British Columbia something should be done right away to meet the situation.

It will be noticed by hon. members tat this item is free; in fact, it has been free for a number of years. There is however a limitation imposed regarding the valuation of the machine, which is set at $3,500. As hon. members know this particular machine is used for digging trenches for farm drainage purposes in which tile drains are laid. Prior to the war these machines were imported free. They are not rMr. Speaker.]
manufactured in Canada; they were not at that time manufactured here and have not been since. The limitation imposed at that time admitted the two smaller sized machines. During the war the price of all commodities rose, as did the price of these machines. The result was that the larger of the two machines admitted was excluded because of this price limitation. The result is that in late years only the smallest machine has been admitted, and those who desired the second largest machine had to purchase a used machine or one which had been rebuilt in the United States and could be imported as a second-hand article. I am asking that the limitation imposed here may be raised from $3,500 to $5,000, which would admit the second size of machine, the same machine that was admitted when this item was first placed on the free list. I remember having this matter before the late Minister of Finance last year; I took it up with his chief tariff advisers, and it was also before the Minister of National Revenue and the commissioner of customs. There has been some difficulty in getting into the country duty free the repairs for the larger size machine; I had this matter up last year with the department in that regard. I believe the only way to remedy this discrepancy and to admit again the machine that at one time was admitted free, would be to raise the limitation from $3,500 to $5,000, and I should like to impress this upon the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman. I think the matter which has been referred to by the hon. member is quite necessary, and something like that ought to be done to get these machines into the country free of duty, as they were admitted for some time up to a certain valuation.

This is purely a matter of revenue; as I understand it, the goods are not made in this country. Moreover, I understand that a case has arisen where one of the machines which came in free required some repairs, and owing to the advance in price the repairs for that machine could not be brought in duty free, although the machine came in free. Now they have to pay duty on the repairs, because to-day the machine is worth more than it was before. This is a case, Mr. Chairman, where we prohibit an article from being made in this country by putting it on the free list, and when the price goes up there is no redress whatever. Put the duty on, and possibly in time you would have them just as cheap here. Here is a case where free trade did not work out exactly as you wanted it bo.

Please use your utmost efforts have kraft and wrapping papers placed on countervailing list in budget. This automatically raises duty five per cent on paper imported from United States. The chairman says:
It is perfectly obvious that you could not have maintained that price if the 5 per cent had not been removed from the domestic car and retained on the imported car.
The matter is I think rather an important one. We were assured by the late Minister of Finance that he would make the manufacturers live up to their promise. The matter has been under consideration by the department for at least two years-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
-and the budget was then brought down and no mention was made of it. I just want to take advantage of this item to ask the minister this question in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In fairness to my predecessor I think I should correct my hon. friend's statement that this matter has been under investigation for two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but he soon found the complicated nature of it and how impossible it was to get at it departmentally. My hon. friend has referred to a letter written I think less than one year ago by my predecessor or, Mr. Robb, to the chairman of the tariff board. I can only say, Mr. Chairman, that earlier in the session, in a discussion directly bearing on this subject, arising out of a resolution introduced I believe by my hon. friend himself, I indicated that I had made inquiries as to the progress of the investigation and reported to the house that the information I received was that the matter was of a very complicated character, that the investigation was proceeding, and that I could not hold out any hope of an early conclusion, especially having regard to the amount of work it was necessary for the Tariff Advisory Board to do in cooperation with myself in the preparation of the budget. The work is proceeding with the aid of outside investigators, all of whom indicate its complexity and the lack of possibility of coming to an immediate conclusion with regard to it. I can assure my hon. friend, however, that it will be pushed along.

speechtext: I am referring to that particular matter specifically.

proven that the manufacturers had been taking a price advantage of the tax. Therefore I thought we might expect some statement from the minister this year in regard to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My advice is that they are not ready to report on any phase of the matter, including the phase to which my hon. friend refers.

In the particular item we are discussing,-and it is a phrase that comes into this tariff in very many instances- there are the words, "and complete parts thereof." Will the minister say just what that means?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am rather embarrassed when asked these administrative questions, especially when they relate to phraseology which has been part of the tariff for many years, and which has acquired a definite administrative meaning. My hon. friend knows that the Minister of Finance does not administer the act. I am under some difficulty in answering him. I can only say that in this case as in all others the words mean exactly what the Customs department in administering the act in the past has interpreted them to mean in relation to similar cases.

I understand that, after all, the Minister of Finance is responsible for the wording of these items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is wrong with this wording?
I am not saying that anything is wrong, but I want to know what these words mean, because two or three meanings can be taken from them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has had a very wide experience, and I am quite sure he knows much better than I do what the standard practice of the Department of National Revenue is in interpreting the expression "and complete parts thereof".

I had an experience last year and the year before with the executive in the customs department, and I am going to be a little more careful in the future, if I am here, to see that no such errors creep in again. I had experience with the way grapes were handled, and I am a little bit suspicious now.
There is a redundancy here; there is no question about that. A part is a part. What is a complete part? Is it not still a part?

Is it a finished
part?
If it is a finished part, why not say so?
I am not saying that it is; I am asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I only know that the phrase has been used in years of customs practice. If the Minister of National Revenue were here he could probably answer, but I have not the necessary knowledge.
The world does move a little.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend does not.
You will find out at the *election whether I do or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon.
The minister is stationary on this item.
In regard to the excise tax on automobiles, would the ministry be good enough to assure the house that the board will give a report on that particular matter before the budget comes down next year?
He will not be here.

I do not think that is asking too much. I have been stalled off in this matter for a long time. The former Minister 
of Finance stalled me off for a year, and then referred the matter to the tariff board. We still have no report from the board although the chairman, whose comment I have just quoted, said that it was perfectly obvious that the Canadian manufacturers could not maintain their price if the 5 per cent had not been removed from the domestic car and retained on the imported car. Will the minister therefore assure us that the board will hurry up and make a report before the next budget comes down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must express my
thanks at the confidence my hon. friend displays that I shall be here to deliver the budget next year. I can assure him that I will do everything humanly possible to get the automobile matter in shape so that parliament can deal with it. More than that I cannot say. There is no object in deliberately holding up investigations of this kind; one desires them to come to a conclusion, particularly if he is in a position of administrative responsibility with regard to them. I have that desire, and I can assure my hon. friend that I shall do the best I can. I hope he will remember that I came into this department only a few months ago and a very short time before the session, and it has not been easy for me to master, even as imperfectly as I have succeeded in doing, the tasks of the department. I can only say I am doing the best I can in regard to it.

Then I would ask the
minister in the very near future while he is still in charge of the department to request the board to endeavour to have a finding made in regard to this matter.

business consists exclusively of the manufacture of these goods. We understand the new budget is intended by its sponsors to help British industries market their products in Canada without retarding or decreasing the sale of Canadian made articles.	.	.
In so far as the electric heating and cooking appliance industry is concerned, this is not so. We believe that budget to be a decided detri- [DOT] ment to our efforts (instead of a help) to increase our business. It is decidedly a "slap in the face" and it is quite possible that the irreparable damage that -was done a few years ago to the Canadian woollen industry, by tariff tinkering, will be repeated-this time the electric heating and cooking appliances industry being the victim.
The following items on the budget affects our industry: Tariff item 443-Apparatus designed for cooking or for heating buildings (3) for electricity. These goods now enter free under the British preferential tariff. Previously there was a duty of 15 per cent. These goods now enjoy reduction of 2i per cent when entering Canada under both the intermediate and general tariffs, from the rates previously in effect. That is. the protection to the Canadian industry on goods entering from Germany and United States is reduced 2J per cent. Easily 75 per cent of the goods that we manufacture are affected by this classification. Now what do we get to compensate?
Tariff item 443a. A reduction of 2J per cent on electric tumbler and rotary switches.
Tariff item 443c. Compensating thermometers a reduction of 5 per cent. These may be imported free from England, but as far as we know there are none made there suitable for our purpose.
The above benefits are more than entirely wiped out bv 21 per cent increase in the duty on strip steel, tariff item 382c, which is now 15 per cent instead of 12J per cent. This type of steel is universally used for all nickel plated steel parts of our product and has been imported from the United States due to superior quality that can be secured. The British preferential and intermediate tariffs on this item remain as before.
No doubt tariff item 3861 is intended to benefit us but it does not. This covers steel sheets, cold rolled blue polished when imported by manufacturers of apparatus designed for cooking or for heating buildings for use in the manufacture of such appliances, and is free when imported from England. This class of steel is not used at all by us nor to any extent by any of our competitors, same being used by the manufacturers of gas, coal and wood ranges. Even if we did use it we doubt if it would be of any assistance, as the increase of uncrating, extra handling, etc., on British steel would offset the saving through the duty on United States manufactured product, as factory to factory carload shipments can be made where no crating is required. The crating of steel for a combination ocean and rail shipment is an expensive item.

We believe that the tariff changes mentioned in the recent budget will very seriously retard the Canadian electrical industry, and more particularly those manufacturers of electrical cooking and heating appliances which can now be imported absolutely free of duty under the British preferential tariff. Britain has long been recognized as a country of manufacturing specialists with centuries of experience, having the world markets well cultivated. It is theie-fore natural that they should enjoy huge production and low' costs.
There is absolutely nothing in the budget that begins to offset the hardships that have been placed on this young Canadian industry. It is interesting to note that the manufacturers ol large electrical machinery, that is generators, transformers, motors, insulators, electrical apparatus, n.o.p., are not affected except that in the latter classification the general tariff has been actually increased 24 per cent, which is probably as it should be. We are simply mentioning this to show that there apparently is no rhyme nor reason for this budget in so far as it affects the electrical heating and cooking appliance industry. There are several small manufacturing plants in Canada specializing in this type of equipment.
The King government apparently is not satisfied with destroving practically three-quarters of the Canadian woollen manufacturing industry. This year they are attempting to cruelty the electric heating and cooking appliance industry, which w-e believe deserves a helping hand instead of the reverse.

The factory at Calgary, as well as the factory at Edmonton, have been depending upon the supply of flour imported from the United States, produced, as I have said, from soft wheat, not from hard wheat. In the province of Ontario the large biscuit factories have ample supplies of flour milled from soft wheat, and the supplies of this commodity going into Alberta come either from Ontario or from the western United States. The demand in Ontario for flour milled from soft wheat is practically met by the home grown article. Importations into Canada from the United States during the last few years have aver-
aged 65,000 barrels per annum, and a duty of 50 cents per barrel has been charged. As it now reads the countervailing duty on soft wheat per barrel will be $2.03.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Two dollars?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, on flour milled from soft wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend sure of his figure?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look at the present American tariff, which does not differentiate between flours milled from hard and soft wheats, he will find my statement to be true. The effect of this will be to impose upon that small industry in Calgary a tax of $2.03 per barrel of flour. Soft wheat flour is practically the only flour which can be utilized for their purposes. I will not repeat what I said the other day as to the difficulties experienced in establishing industries in these western communities. I could cite the case of the Regal biscuit factory which lost something like $300,000 when it went out of business in western Canada. It was established in the city of Calgary. Through local capital efforts are now being made to reestablish the industry. The investment involved in the city of Calgary amounts to about $300,000, and there are approximately 125 employees on the payroll.
Notwithstanding the protection that has been afforded to Canadian industry the importation of unsweetened biscuits from the United States during the fiscal year 1924-25 amounted to 612,000 pounds; in 1925-26, 706,000 pounds; in 1926-27, 733,000 pounds; in 1927-28, 864,000 pounds, and in 1928-29, 881,000 pounds. The importations of the sweetened product from the United States increased from 347,000 pounds in 1924 to 1,105,459 pounds in 1928-29. In the intervening years the importation had reached as high as 1,280,000 pounds, and the low figure was 998.000 pounds. Under the proposed countervailing duty against all classes of flour there will be a duty of $2.03 per barrel instead of 50 cents per barrel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes. I am basing my
figure on 196 pounds to the barrel. I submit to the minister that the purpose he has in mind would be amply fulfilled by sub-dividing the item so as to provide for countervailing duties on hard wheat flour, and an additional clause in connection with soft wheat flour. I would suggest the addition to item 61a as follows:

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Wheat flour, of soft wheat, when imported by manufacturers of biscuits for use only in their own factories in the manufacture of biscuits, per barrel: British preferential tariff, free:	intermediate tariff, 50 cents; general
tariff, 50 cents.
Such an addition would have the effect of enabling this industry to continue, while at the same time it would not in any sense interfere with the operation of the countervailing duties in connection with the class of wheat flour covered by the tariff item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend
investigated the freight rate situation from the point of origin of the soft wheat flour?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should have said to my hon. friend that so far as freight rates are concerned there is no milling in transit rate on soft wheat flour from eastern Canada to Calgary, therefore the milling in transit rate that applies to eastbound traffic has no application. Whereas the wheat at one time was ground in small quantities in the mill at Enderby which has since been abandoned, as some of the hon. gentlemen will no doubt recall, and there being no soft wheat grown in the prairie provinces suitable for the production of biscuits, we have to have recourse to the supply in the States directly south of Alberta. I refer to the state of Washington-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Farther south than that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Washington?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, and probably a little farther south on some occasions. Special varieties of soft wheat flour may be obtained farther south than Washington and Oregon, but in the main those states produce the flour which is used in the Calgary plant for biscuit making. So far as I can see there would be no Canadian industry or activity affected by my proposed item. If there were it is needless to say I should be very glad to have such industries protected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The milling of soft wheat flour is an important Canadian industry.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But only where there is
a constant and ever increasing demand nearby, because the freight rate makes it impossible to move the wheat west. I tell the minister frankly that so far as my investigation has gone I have stated the facts correctly. A representative of a western plant came down here to interview the minister, but I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has had an opportunity to confer with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My office was in touch
with him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of course he feels that the increase in duty from 50 cents to $2.03, on a product which is not produced in his part of Canada and which under existing freight rates cannot be made available for the development of that industry, there being no milling in transit rate on westbound products, is an impossible situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I mentioned the freight rate aspect of it having in mind the present source of supply and the rate on the product to Calgary and Edmonton and I believe also to Regina, where I think there is a branch of the same institution, although I am not sure. As nearly as I could work it out without accurately and definitely getting the rates, it should be possible to ship that flour from the east to the west at a comparable rate to that which prevails from the point of origin in the United States. However, I do not expect to deal completely with the resolution to-night and perhaps I might make a note to look into this matter further; the item as such is passed, but the resolution itself will not be passed until all the component parts have been dealt with. I will look further into the matter. My hon. friend's suggestion is a qualification. Of course so far as Ontario is concerned he will appreciate the fact that the item as it stands is very acceptable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes. If it affected in that province any trade with the community to which I have referred, then of course there would be clear justification for protection of the indutsry-that is the industry of agriculture-by the application of the tariff item. But from 50 cents to $2.03 a barrel is an increase of something like 300 per cent on that item alone, and if it were pure protection the rate would not be necessary. It is more than that; it is an incidence to the application of a countervailing duty on wheat flour, which should be divided into two classes, namely that produced from soft wheat and that produced from hard wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend sees the difficulty, of course, but I will give it further consideration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: To save time I have purposely discussed the matter now, having mentioned it to the minister, rather than when the measure based upon these items was submitted.

These are the items in
connection with which the leader of the opposition made a suggestion. I have looked into it and I find that it would be quite impracticable in operation, as far as I can gather from trying to follow what would be the result. It would produce in practice a chaotic condition in relation to three or four items of the customs tariff, and particularly as applied to a number of industries in different parts of Canada, some of which might be complying with the conditions while others were not, whereas the tariff itself is applicable across the whole of Canada and to all imports of that class or kind. It would be quite impossible of application.

Might I suggest that these
items be held over until to-morrow morning? Quite a number of members would like to discuss them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have been standing now for two or three days following a very elaborate discussion, and there is half an hour yet remaining to-night. I should like to
ask the minister if he has reconsidered item 296.
[The Chairman.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are gathering still
information on feldspar, and that item either will have to be carried as it is or will have to stand for the moment. It is very hard for my officers to get sufficient time to prepare information for me while they are compelled to be in the house.
Shall item 377 carry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What the minister has
said probably is true, except that perhaps those who might be affected could give some assurance that they will look into the question of improving the conditions under which labour is now employed. I fancy there will be no difficulty about that being said. I did look into the matter, as the minister suggested, and I have some doubt as to the validity of any such amendment, from the standpoint of interfering with the scheme of taxation, in view of what the chairman said the other day. That is the reason, frankly, why it was not embodied in the form of an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend
looked into the practicability of it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have not up to the
moment done more than look into the other aspect of it, the one in which I was more intimately concerned, having regard to what the chairman said the other day.

I do not think this ought to carry. We tried to impress upon the committee the other day the importance of protecting the interests of the workers in the steel industry. I do not think it is necessary at this stage to review what was then said. The fact is that these companies are receiving a very considerable benefit from this country and the least we should do is to insist that their employees be given something like decent conditions under which to work.
It has been stated that the company is not at the moment in a very good position to give this assurance. That statement has been made for a good many years now. For the past six or seven years I have discussed this matter in the house, and always we are told that the companies are not in a position to do it. I have never yet heard of a reform which has not been met with some statement of that kind. It seems to me that the time has come when we have to decide frankly whether dividends or the needs of the employees are to have first consideration. It may be said in this connection that the company is not .paying dividends. At least it is carrying on, and I take it that in a good many departments we already recognize that wages are a first claim. It ought to be

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
recognized here that wages and decent working conditions are a first claim upon the industry. I quoted figures the other day to show that provision was being made for the obsolescence of machinery, for replacement, for reserves, and so on. I have no objection to the company making such provisions, but I do say that provision ought to be made for the people whom it employs, and that the provision for the employees ought to come first.
Under these circumstances I think the Prime Minister ought to accede to our request. He said that if we took the step in this case it would have to be taken in all cases, and he said also that he was willing to do it. I should like to have him make a statement on that particular point. I think he should do so, after what was said on the floor of the house the other day. I quite concede that it might be difficult to apply immediately in industry the whole of the provisions of the treaty of Versailles, and that is why I am in favour of having some of them applied in this one item. I quite concede that all industrial establishments ought to have the eight hour day, but these Steel works are the only big industrial establishments I know of in this country that are working their men twelve hours a day.
And fourteen hours per day.

They work twelve hours a day for seven days in t.he week, and in some cases the night men work thirteen hours a shift. During the change over from shift to shift I am told that the men work for twenty-four hours without cessation. So far as I know this is the only large industry in which men have to work under such conditions; hence there is a particular reason for the making of suitable provisions in this case. When protection is being given to this industry, provision should be made for the workers. Why put it off until another year has passed? Is the government going to put this off altogether? Why wait until such time as the companies are prepared to come through?

Mr. Chairman, I desire to make a statement in regard to the remarks made the other night in reference to this matter. On Wednesday night the house heard a good deal of lurid speech as to living and labour conditions in Glace Bay, Cape Breton. Quotations were made from reported investigations by certain well-meaning men of God and others with what perhaps may be termed somewhat advanced views as to
social service and similar matters. Some of the statements quoted and made were probably correct; others were possibly exaggerations.
I have no interest in the Besco corporation and never had beyond a small matter of holding shares to the nominal value of 8100 with a present market value of less than half that amount. As to the condition of their housing properties at Glace Bay, I personally know nothing and therefore offer neither criticism nor defence.
In view of the general denouncement voiced here last Wednesday night, I consider it desirable now to say that conditions such as referred to do not now prevail nor have they at any time during the past forty-five years prevailed as regards the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company of New Glasgow, in connection with either their mainland or their Cape Breton enterprises. Neither at New Glasgow nor at Trenton did that company build or own any houses or tenements for the housing of its employees. They did, however, encourage and assist employees to build and own their houses, and many of them do own their houses in both these towns, due to assistance given by the company.
When the Scotia Company acquired in 1900 the property and mines of the General Mining Association of London, and in the following year proceeded to develop further the property by opening additional collieries and erecting coal washeries, coke ovens, blast furnaces and a modern open hearth steel plant, they found the colliery employees for the most part living in houses many of which had been occupied for many years. Some of these of brick and stone construction were in fairly good condition and comfortable. On the other hand a considerable number of the wooden houses were not in good condition. These were replaced by upwards of 350 new houses, all of which were supplied with water and sewer connection and electric lighting facilities, and the occupants were urged to and in many cases have become owners, the company selling the houses to employees at actual cost and payment being made by monthly contributions with interest at 6 per cent on the outstanding balances. Most, if indeed not all, of these houses are now owned outright and free from any liability to the company. A considerable number of houses were also built on plots of suitable land situate on the established streets, with water, sewer and electric connections, the land being given to the operatives free of cost if the employee built a house thereon, the cost being advanced at 6 per cent interest, repayable at the convenience of the employee owners.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
No such conditions as described on Wednesday night exist or at any time have existed at New Glasgow, Trenton or Sydney Mines in so far as the employees of the Scotia Company were or are concerned. I make this statement without fear of successful contradiction and from first-hand knowledge gained by official connection with the corporation for more than two score years and as its general manager and director for more than twenty years.
May I add that from the formation of the Scotia Company the value of a contented, loyal body of workers was recognized and fostered by the management, and a more skilful and enthusiastic group of coal miners and steel operators than those of the Scotia's employ do not exist anywhere. Leaders have been supplied from those workers to many similar undertakings both in Canada and in the United States. The success of the ideal to which I refer is evidenced by the fact that in the case of the mainland enterprise, which has operated continuously for more than fifty years, and in the case of the Sydney Mines coal and steel operations, carried on over a period of thirty years, no strike has ever occurred. True it is that on one brief occasion during the overstrained period of the war a ticket-of-leave Australian convict agitator appeared and succeeded in stirring up some little friction. That, however, was speedily settled by mutual agreement and with no stoppage of work and no shadow of unrest or suggestion of dissatisfaction has since developed-a record, Mr. Chairman, which I claim to be creditable both to the men and to the management, a record not excelled by any corporation in this Dominion operating a like diversified industry. During the period I have referred to, other corporations in Nova Scotia, both coal mining and steel companies, have had several severe and long continued strikes. One company within a period of twenty-five years has had more than a score of strikes. Another corporation had a stoppage of its operations extending considerably over a year -indeed, approaching two full years. The experience of the Scotia Company in that connection is, I submit, most illuminating, and so far as that corporation is concerned the denunciations of the various speakers on Wednesday evening last do not apply.
I am glad to have had the opportunity of making this statement, and I think it only fair to the corporation to which I have referred and to the workers employed by it that the committee should be in possession of the actual facts.
Which speakers are you referring to?
To some of the speakers who spoke on Wednesday evening.
What speakers?
I am not going to particularize them.

Will the hon. gentleman be
good enough to inform the committee as to the number of hours worked by the men employed at the mill at New Glasgow?
I think the longest hours we have worked in recent years is a fifty-four hour week.

Are there night and day
shifts?
I think so.

Do any of the men in the
steel mills work the same hours as they do at Sydney?
I do not know what hours are worked at Sydney.
Does the night shift at New Glasgow work twelve hours?
Not that I know of.
New Glasgow was not mentioned in any of the denouncements made on Wednesday evening.
I agree with that.

We were referring particularly to conditions which are well known to exist at Glace Bay and Sydney. I do not think there is one hon. member of this house who would dispute the statements made in reference to those places, which statements have been made not only this year but in previous years. I think it is a little unfair for the previous speaker (Mr. Cantley) to throw suspicion upon the men and women of high reputation who went to the mills at Sydney and Glace Bay and investigated the conditions existing there, which conditions were condemned in the strongest possible language. Severe condemnation of these conditions was made also by the commission appointed by the government of Nova Scotia. I do not think there is a single hon. member who would dare to rise in his place and defend the conditions which exist at the steel mills of the Besco corporation. I must confess that I know very little about the conditions at New Glasgow, but neither I nor any other hon. member mentioned those particular works when this matter was under discussion.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
I had hoped, when the leader of the opposition and the leader of the house were unanimous in saying that better conditions should be provided for 'the men engaged in the steel industry in particular, there would have been some action on the part of the government. But what do we find? To-night the Minister of Finance, without adequate reason asks us to adopt a measure of increased protection to the British Empire Steel Corporation. What was the defence of the minister Wednesday evening? It was that the employees themselves had asked for this protection. Hon. members who are familiar with the conditions that prevail in the steel industry will realize how easy it is, with the company union they have, to pay the expenses of the men to Ottawa in order that they may plead on behalf of the company.
May I point out to the minister and to the committee a more classic -example than that of these men who came here and pleaded for the company? Those who have read the history of the civil war of the United States know how the slaves, who were mere chattels, fought on the side of their masters when the north was trying to emancipate them from chattel slavery. We have similar conditions to-day when an attempt is being made to free men from what might be called wage slavery. Even the men themselves object to the eight hour day, because they think for the moment it may mean a reduction in pay. I am surprised, however, that the Minister of Finance, who ought to know something of conditions in poor homes, who has risen from a humble home to the position he now occupies, should defend an increase-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must object to that. I was merely giving information to the committee. If my hon. friend will read what I said, he will not find in it any cause for surprise. It is my duty to give information and I merely gave it without comment; in fadt, I specifically so stated.
I would be the last person in the world to do an injustice to the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My concluding remarks were:
What concerns me is how it is possible practically and definitely to apply it, and that feature of the matter, of course, requires consideration. I rose merely to advise the committee that the men had associated themselves unconditionally with the employers in asking for what is here granted.

But the Minister of Finance was trying to pilot through the house increased protection for this industry, and one 2419-158
of the reasons he gave to the house in support of the proposal was that the men themselves employed in the steel industry had agreed to this increased tariff protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The men stated that they desired it, and I merely conveyed that information to the house.

I do not know whom the men Who desired it represented; they may or may not have represented all the men in the industry. But I have also had an opportunity of coming into contact with those men and I know that to-day they are complaining most bitterly of the conditions under which they are compelled to work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no doubt of it,
and properly so.

If they want redress, how are they to get it? They find it almost impossible to organize. Everything the company by strong organization can use against them is being so used. The only place to which they can look for redress is parliament. What is parliament doing? Instead of looking after the interests of the men it is looking after the interests of the owners of the industry, the capitalists; it is giving protection to the industry, and the men can wait until it suits the employers to give better conditions to their employees. It is common knowledge that in the past couple of days, since we had this discussion on Wednesday, there have been around these buildings some of the directors of the British Empire Steel Corporation. I have no objection to their coming here and pleading with their friends in the house; but how different would conditions be if the men had an opportunity of coming here. It is, however, difficult for them to come; they cannot afford to do so unless under the same conditions as the men came last year, their expenses being paid by the company, and pleaded for higher protection for the industry.
To-night I am making a plea for the men. At the moment I am not concerned as to the financial position of the corporation. I know there exist in the city of Sydney in the Dominion of Canada conditions which are a disgrace to this country, where men are compelled to work on night shifts thirteen hours at a stretch with an interval of only half an hour for something to eat, and where some weeks they work 102 hours. It is almost unheard-of; it is well-nigh unbelievable. To-night I was in a friend's house in Ottawa and the lady of the house said to me: "I read something in the newspaper about men working eleven and twelve hours a day. Surely they would

Unemployment in Alberta

not work eleven and twelve hours a day in the Dominion of Canada!" I had to tell her that men not only had to do that, but that on some shifts they had to work thirteen hours at a stretch.
Further, if an industry as wealthy as the British Empire Steel Corporation, with all the advantages it has at its command, cannot afford to provide for its men better conditions than those, Canada would in the long run be better off without such an industry. Can the industry afford to give those men better conditions? Rarely has there been an industry that of its own volition has given conditions to its employees. Parliament therefore takes a retrograde step if it gives protection to the shareholders who live in all parts of the world and refuses to give a little bit of protection to the men employed in the industry. We all admit that conditions under which men are compelled to work eleven, twelve and thirteen hours at a stretch, are intolerable. Our first duty therefore is not toward the shareholders but toward the man; yet we are not taking any action that would appear to afford better conditions to the men engaged in the industry. The other night hon. members representing those districts and representing the workers in Nova Scotia rose in their places and pleaded with the house that some action be taken.
Progress reported.
